title: Improvised drummers across the South and the white drummer sent home
summary: From Columbia, South Carolina, to Tampa they use whatever drummer they can find, while the distressed white New Yorker is sent back.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Our next dance was in South Carolina. I think it was in the capital of South Carolina...

Columbia, South Carolina. And when we got down there, we were rushing around to find a drummer. Now, the Army has got just about anybody who can do anything, whether they're a drummer or a carpenter. It's hard to find anybody that can do anything! Nevertheless, they scrounge around and they found some old fellow that... I think he had played with the Elks band or something, and he had played years ago but he hadn't played for a long time. So that night he came on the

bandstand with this great, big bass drum, which had a picture of a moon and a river on it... Heh-heh... He just had an odd-looking set of drums with him. If anything, it was this big bass drum... So everybody's saying, "Oh my God, what's going to happen?" But at least he made a picture of we're having a drummer, plus hopefully that he might be able to play with some kind of beat.

So with Dizzy up there, and the brass section sitting next to him, coaxing him and trying to tell him when to play and when not to play, we made it through the night. That took care of Columbia, South Carolina. And that went on for two or three nights, heading South, even in Atlanta, Georgia. We would pick up some leftover drummer or somebody who had a set of drums or something like that, and try to make it. And finally, we got to Tampa, Florida, and we found a young kid down there, I can't remember his name either.... But he could play fairly well.

Incidentally, I'd like to mention the fact that this White Boy that we had with us, that played the job with us in Wilmington and Washington, he was very unhappy. He was just frustrated, because he'd never been in no situation like that, and he was a New York boy, and just never had no idea that you could ever run up against a situation where he couldn't do what he wanted to, or couldn't be with who he wanted to. I

guess it was my first look at how somebody would react to segregation in reverse. He was very mad, and he told Billy that... He acted as if, if Billy had let him stay, that he would make it all right, that he'd show these people down there. So Billy told him, you know, "Well, what you'll do is go down and get yourself killed and all of us." Finally, he reluctantly went back to New York.
